episode.episode: Philips Hue: The smart home’s light bulb moment
episode.showDescription: Version History is a show about the best gadgets ever. And the worst ones. And the ones that might have changed the world, if they ever actually shipped. Every week, your favorite people from The Verge and beyond hang out to tell and debate the story of a gadget, app, website, or any other tech product, and try to determine the item’s true legacy. Because not every product is a hit, but every product has a story. And the ones that really matter aren’t always the ones you think. From the Verge and the Vox Media Podcast Network.
episode.episodeDescription: The humble light bulb might be the ultimate success story in the smart home. Our connected, adaptable homes are supposed to be customizable, connected to everything, and incredibly easy to use, and nothing has made that work quite like Philips Hue lights. In this episode, The Verge's David Pierce and Jennifer Pattison Tuohy are joined by smart home journalist and expert Richard Gunther to tell the Hue's story. We trace the product's history from its origins in the smartphone revolution, try to figure out how Philips managed to turn a staggeringly expensive lightbulb into a must-have gadget, and look at whether there's even more invention left in the future of lighting. We’re also on video! Check us out on YouTube. Subscribe to The Verge for unlimited access to theverge.com, subscriber-exclusive newsletters, and our ad-free podcast feed. We love hearing from you! transcript_window.text: And Color Kinetics is still around, and it's the company that, like, lights up the Empire State Building and does stuff like that.
Very cool company and a very smart acquisition on Philips' part.
Yeah, that's again, Philips, deeply fascinating company.
And everything you can imagine Philips has made at one point or another.

Yeah, the one other bit of the tech that I saw that I thought was really cool is they were having trouble managing the radio that you need to connect to actually get signals to and from the bulb because the heat sinks that they were using to keep the bulbs cool were actually interfering with
the radio frequency.
So what they did was they— Turns when you put a radio in a big metal thing, it's hard for it to actually communicate.
But what they find a way to do is actually attach the two pieces together.
And so they turned the heat sink essentially into the antenna and actually managed to make it work for them instead of against them.
But again, as far as I can tell, it is a minor miracle that any of this worked at all.
Absolutely.
Absolutely.
Absolutely.

And, you know, while we're talking about those heat sinks, one of the things that was problematic for LED lighting in the beginning was that that heat sink took up all the bottom space of a light bulb.
So typically when you went to the hardware store to buy a very expensive LED light bulb that was probably terrible, it only shined light upwards.
Yeah.
Because it only had the top part with a lens on it that exposed the light.
Right.
What Philips did was brilliant in shaping the lens portion of the bulb in a way that it actually cast light out and down, not just up.
Yeah.
And today we don't have them here, but the current hue bulbs are fully glass.
Right.
Yeah, they just look like light bulbs.
They just look like regular light bulbs.
Yeah, it was actually kind of wild coming into the studio and seeing how much these don't look like light bulbs.

There was a wired story when these first ones came out that called them smushed ice cream tons, which I think is exactly the mental image that everyone should have in their mind if you're listening to this.
